source.title: What Lies Beneath
source.summary: The resource curse, Dutch disease, critical minerals, and the Islamic concept of communal resource ownership.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Countries that discover oil or minerals often end up worse off, not better. The resource curse is one of the most robust findings in development economics: resource wealth weakens institutions, concentrates power, and crowds out productive sectors through Dutch disease. This episode covers the mechanism, the evidence, and the exceptions (Norway, Botswana). Then it turns to Islamic resource economics: the fay' principle that communal resources belong to the community, the hima system of protected commons, and how sovereign wealth funds (particularly the Gulf model) represent a partial modern application. Pakistan's critical minerals reserves make this directly relevant. The honest assessment: Islamic principles point in the right direction, but no Muslim-majority resource economy has fully solved the institutional challenge.

thread: Countries that discover oil often end up poorer than before they found it. The resource curse is one of the most reliable patterns in development economics.
Oil money weakens institutions and crowds out other industries through Dutch disease. Manufacturing dies when your currency gets too strong from resource exports.
Only a few countries escaped this trap. Norway and Botswana managed to turn resource wealth into lasting prosperity instead of temporary booms.

Islamic economics has the fay' principle: communal resources belong to the community, not rulers. Pakistan's critical minerals could test whether this works in practice. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-trt-4

linkedin.post: One of the most counterintuitive findings in development economics is the resource curse: countries that discover oil or minerals often end up worse off, not better. The mechanism is well-documented—resource wealth weakens institutions, concentrates power, and crowds out productive sectors through Dutch disease. Only a few countries like Norway and Botswana have escaped this trap. What did they do differently? They built strong institutions before the resource boom hit. Islamic economics offers an interesting perspective through the fay' principle: communal resources belong to the community, not the state. The Gulf's sovereign wealth funds represent a partial modern application of this concept. With Pakistan sitting on significant critical minerals reserves, we have a real-time test case for whether these principles can translate into practice. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-trt-4

instagram.caption: Countries that strike oil often end up poorer, not richer. It's called the resource curse, and it's one of the most reliable patterns economists have found. Here's what happens: Oil money weakens institutions, concentrates power with rulers, and kills other industries through "Dutch disease" - when your currency gets too strong from resource exports that manufacturing dies. Only Norway and Botswana really escaped this trap. They built strong institutions first. Islamic economics has something interesting to offer here: the fay' principle says communal resources belong to the community, not the state. Gulf sovereign wealth funds are a partial example of this in practice. Pakistan's critical minerals could be the next test case.
